title: Candidate keys and alternate keys
description: A practical guide to separating all possible row identifiers from the one chosen as the primary key, using a hypothetical customer table with counterexamples.
lead: Candidate keys are the identifiers that could uniquely name rows in a relation. The primary key is the candidate key selected as the main identifier. Alternate keys are the remaining candidate keys that were not selected as primary. The distinction matters because a table can have several valid identifiers, but the model still needs one principal reference point for ordinary joins, foreign keys, and human reasoning.

sections.heading: The short version
paragraphs: A superkey is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: it is unique, and no attribute can be removed without losing that uniqueness. A primary key is the candidate key selected as the table’s principal identifier. An alternate key is a candidate key that was not selected as primary.

This is a modeling distinction before it is an implementation detail. PostgreSQL can enforce primary key and unique constraints, and its documentation describes a primary key as unique and not null. But the modeler still has to decide which facts are stable enough to be identifiers and which facts only look unique in today’s sample data.

For example, a customer table might have a generated customer_id, an account_email, and a loyalty_card_number. If all three are required and unique by business rule, each may be a candidate key. If the model chooses customer_id as the primary key, then account_email and loyalty_card_number are alternate keys. If email can be reused, missing, shared, or corrected in a way that creates duplicate rows at this table’s grain, it is not a candidate key even if it is unique in a small extract.
bullets: Superkey: any unique row identifier, possibly with extra columns.
Candidate key: a minimal superkey.
Primary key: the candidate key chosen as the main identifier.
Alternate key: a candidate key not chosen as primary.

sections.heading: A hypothetical customer fixture
paragraphs: Use this small hypothetical retail customer relation. The goal is not to design a complete customer model. The goal is to separate possible identifiers from the selected identifier.

Assume the intended relation has one row per registered customer. The business has assigned each customer a stable internal customer_id. Each registered customer must have exactly one account_email and one loyalty_card_number. For this fixture, both account_email and loyalty_card_number are required to be unique among registered customers.

Under those assumptions, three single-column attributes identify a customer: customer_id, account_email, and loyalty_card_number. Each is unique. Each is minimal because no smaller subset exists than one column. Therefore, each is a candidate key. If the data model chooses customer_id as the primary key, then account_email and loyalty_card_number are alternate keys.

The phrase “under those assumptions” is doing real work. Candidate keys come from semantics, not from a lucky profile of one dataset. If the rule is “current email is unique and required,” account_email can identify the current registered customer row even though the address may be changed later. If email history is stored in the same relation, email probably stops identifying one current customer row. If loyalty cards can be missing or reassigned, loyalty_card_number is not a candidate key for this relation.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style DDL for the hypothetical fixture.
-- This is a modeling example, not an execution result.

CREATE TABLE registered_customer (
    customer_id          integer PRIMARY KEY,
    account_email        text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    loyalty_card_number  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    full_name            text NOT NULL,
    signup_date          date NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO registered_customer
    (customer_id, account_email, loyalty_card_number, full_name, signup_date)
VALUES
    (101, 'avery.rivera@example.test', 'LC-7001', 'Avery Rivera', DATE '2026-01-04'),
    (102, 'blair.shah@example.test',   'LC-7002', 'Blair Shah',   DATE '2026-01-05'),
    (103, 'casey.morgan@example.test', 'LC-7003', 'Casey Morgan', DATE '2026-01-07');

sections.heading: Counterexamples that look like keys
paragraphs: Many modeling errors start when a column is treated as a key because it is unique in a sample. The sample may be clean, incomplete, or too small to show the real rule. Here are four common counterexamples using the same hypothetical customer context.

First, full_name is not a key. In the three-row fixture, full_name happens to be unique. But names do not identify registered customers under ordinary retail assumptions. Two customers can share the same name, and one customer can change a name. Uniqueness in the current rows is not enough.

Second, signup_date is not a key. It is not unique in the intended domain. Even if this sample has different dates, many customers can sign up on the same date. A date may help describe a customer; it does not identify one.

Third, customer_id plus account_email is a superkey but not a candidate key. The pair is unique because customer_id is already unique. However, account_email can be removed and the remaining customer_id still identifies the row. That makes the pair non-minimal. It is a superkey with an unnecessary passenger.

Fourth, account_email may fail as a candidate key if the business rule changes. Suppose guest checkout rows, family accounts, or historical email records are added to the same relation. If account_email can be null, shared, or repeated over time, it is not a candidate key for that relation. It may belong in a separate relation with its own grain and validity rules.
bullets: A column that is unique in a sample is only a candidate key if the business rule guarantees uniqueness for the relation.
Adding extra columns to an already unique identifier creates a superkey, not a candidate key.
A descriptive attribute can be important for analytics while still being invalid as an identifier.
When the grain changes, old keys may stop being keys.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostic queries for the hypothetical fixture.
-- These queries find duplicate values in possible single-column identifiers.
-- A zero-row result is necessary evidence, but not sufficient proof, of a candidate key.

SELECT account_email, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM registered_customer
GROUP BY account_email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT loyalty_card_number, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM registered_customer
GROUP BY loyalty_card_number
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

SELECT full_name, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM registered_customer
GROUP BY full_name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

sections.heading: How to classify possible identifiers
paragraphs: A practical way to classify identifiers is to start with the relation’s grain, then test each possible identifier against uniqueness, requiredness, minimality, and stability. These checks are conceptual first. Data profiling can reveal violations, but it cannot by itself define the business rule.

Step one: state the grain. For the example table, the grain is one row per registered customer. Without this sentence, the key conversation is ambiguous. An email may identify a current registered customer, an email address record, a login credential, or a message recipient depending on the table.

Step two: list plausible identifiers. In the hypothetical fixture, the plausible identifiers are customer_id, account_email, and loyalty_card_number. Less plausible attributes such as full_name and signup_date can still be examined, but they should not be promoted merely because they look unique today.

Step three: check uniqueness against the intended domain. A key must identify at most one row. If the organization allows two registered customers to share an email address, account_email is not a candidate key. If it does not allow sharing, and the table stores only the current email for each registered customer, then account_email can be a candidate key.

Step four: check requiredness. PostgreSQL primary key constraints require values to be both unique and not null. PostgreSQL unique constraints enforce uniqueness, but their default null treatment allows more than one row with a null in at least one constrained column. Practically, if a supposed key can be missing, it is not a reliable identifier for the relation unless the design explicitly handles that case.

Step five: check minimality. If customer_id alone identifies a row, then customer_id plus account_email is not a candidate key. It is still unique, but it is not minimal. Minimality prevents bloated identifiers that make foreign keys wider and obscure the real dependency.

Step six: select one primary key. The selected primary key should be stable, compact enough to reference, and aligned with how dependent tables will point to this relation. The other candidate keys do not disappear. They remain alternate keys and should be documented and, where appropriate, constrained.

sections.heading: Primary key choice does not erase alternate keys
paragraphs: Choosing customer_id as the primary key does not mean account_email and loyalty_card_number are unimportant. It means customer_id is the identifier the model uses as the principal reference. Alternate keys still express business rules: no two registered customers can have the same current account email, and no two registered customers can have the same loyalty card number.

This distinction prevents two opposite mistakes. The first mistake is using every unique field as if it were the primary key. That leads to inconsistent joins: one pipeline joins orders to customers by customer_id, another joins events by email, and a third joins rewards activity by loyalty card. When the values change or arrive late, the model has no single anchor.

The second mistake is enforcing only the primary key and ignoring alternate keys. If customer_id is unique but account_email is allowed to duplicate accidentally, the table may still satisfy its primary key constraint while violating the business rule that each current account email belongs to one registered customer. The primary key protects selected row identity; alternate keys protect other valid identifiers.

In SQL, a common implementation is a primary key constraint for the selected key and unique constraints for alternate keys. That maps well to the concept but is not the whole design. The model should also record what the alternate key means: current email, verified email, login email, billing email, active loyalty card, or something else. Without that meaning, the constraint name may be correct while the data model remains unclear.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative implementation of one primary key and two alternate keys.
-- Constraint names make the modeling decision explicit.

CREATE TABLE registered_customer (
    customer_id          integer NOT NULL,
    account_email        text NOT NULL,
    loyalty_card_number  text NOT NULL,
    full_name            text NOT NULL,
    signup_date          date NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT pk_registered_customer
        PRIMARY KEY (customer_id),

    CONSTRAINT ak_registered_customer_account_email
        UNIQUE (account_email),

    CONSTRAINT ak_registered_customer_loyalty_card_number
        UNIQUE (loyalty_card_number)
);

sections.heading: Join semantics and foreign keys
paragraphs: Keys also shape how tables relate. Suppose a hypothetical order table has one row per order and stores customer_id. A foreign key from customer_order.customer_id to registered_customer.customer_id says each order references the selected customer identifier. The join condition follows the modeled relationship, not whichever customer attribute happens to be available in an event feed.

If an upstream source supplies only account_email, that does not make account_email the primary key. It means the ingestion process may need to resolve account_email to customer_id using the alternate key. The alternate key is useful because it gives a safe lookup path while preserving customer_id as the table’s primary reference.

This is where candidate keys and alternate keys become practical for data engineering. They make joins intentional. Joining orders to customers on full_name is invalid even if a profiling query shows no duplicate names today. Joining on account_email can be valid if account_email is an enforced alternate key and the business meaning is current customer email. Joining on customer_id is usually preferred when the dependent table already carries that primary identifier.

PostgreSQL’s table expression documentation describes joined tables as tables derived from two source tables according to the join type and join condition. The database can evaluate the predicate you write, but it cannot infer your business grain from a coincidental attribute. The data model has to supply that meaning.

PostgreSQL also allows a foreign key to reference columns that are a primary key, columns that form a unique constraint, or columns from a non-partial unique index. That means an alternate key can be a valid referenced identifier in PostgreSQL when it is declared appropriately. Even then, the modeling question remains: should this dependent table point to the selected primary identifier, or is the alternate identifier the relationship the table really stores?

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical dependent table using the selected primary identifier.
-- This is illustrative SQL, not an execution result.

CREATE TABLE customer_order (
    order_id     integer PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  integer NOT NULL,
    order_date   date NOT NULL,
    order_total  numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT fk_customer_order_registered_customer
        FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES registered_customer (customer_id)
);

-- If a source event arrives with only an email address, the alternate key can resolve it.
-- This is illustrative SQL, not an execution result.

SELECT
    e.source_event_id,
    c.customer_id,
    e.event_time
FROM source_email_event AS e
JOIN registered_customer AS c
  ON c.account_email = e.account_email;

sections.heading: A practical diagnostic for your own model
paragraphs: When reviewing a table, write down each possible identifier in four columns: unique, required, minimal, and stable for this relation. Then classify it as primary key, alternate key, non-minimal superkey, or not a key. This small exercise often exposes hidden grain problems.

For the hypothetical registered_customer relation, the diagnostic looks like this in prose. customer_id is unique, required, minimal, and stable, so it is a candidate key and the selected primary key. account_email is unique, required, and minimal under the stated rule, so it is a candidate key and an alternate key. loyalty_card_number is also a candidate key and an alternate key under the stated rule. customer_id plus account_email is unique but not minimal, so it is a superkey but not a candidate key. full_name is not guaranteed unique, so it is not a key. signup_date is not unique and not a key.

The most useful part of the diagnostic is not the label itself. It is the argument behind the label. If two engineers disagree about whether account_email is an alternate key, the disagreement should move to the rule: Can a registered customer lack an email? Can two customers share one? Are historical emails stored in this table? Can an email be reassigned to a different customer record? Once those questions are answered, the key classification usually becomes straightforward.

Do not let implementation shortcuts decide the model silently. A generated integer can be an excellent primary key, but it does not remove the need to constrain natural alternate identifiers. A natural identifier can be a valid primary key, but it should still be judged for stability and meaning. The core question is always the same: which attributes identify one row at this table’s grain, and which one will the model choose as the main reference?
bullets: Start with the table grain before naming keys.
Treat sample uniqueness as evidence to investigate, not as proof.
A primary key is selected from candidate keys; it is not the only possible identifier by definition.
Alternate keys should be documented and usually enforced when the database supports the rule.
Non-minimal unique combinations are superkeys, not candidate keys.

takeaways: Candidate keys are all minimal identifiers for a relation; the primary key is the one chosen as the principal identifier.
Alternate keys are not second-class data. They are candidate keys that still express business rules even though they were not selected as primary.
A unique-looking column is not automatically a key. It must match the table grain, be required, be unique by rule, and be minimal.
Adding columns to an already unique identifier creates a non-minimal superkey, not a better candidate key.
Use constraints and clear names to make primary and alternate key decisions visible in the schema.

title: Functional dependencies in analytical tables
description: Use functional dependency violations to find analytical attributes stored at the wrong grain, with a small hypothetical order-line dataset and an illustrative SQL diagnostic.
lead: Functional dependencies are a practical way to ask whether an attribute belongs at the grain where it is stored. In an analytical table, a violation often points to a column that is being treated as stable at one level of detail even though the data says it changes at another.

sections.heading: The grain question behind a dependency
paragraphs: A functional dependency says that one set of attributes determines another attribute. If customer_id determines customer_name, then every row with the same customer_id should have the same customer_name. If product_id determines product_category, then every row with the same product_id should have the same product_category.

The useful practitioner question is not only whether the dependency passes. It is: when the same determinant has more than one dependent value, what grain is the dependent attribute really stored at? A dependency violation is a counterexample to a grain assumption.

Analytical tables often repeat descriptive attributes for convenience. A fact table at order-line grain may contain order_date, customer_id, product_id, customer_tier, product_category, and category_manager. Repetition alone is not the problem. A single order_date repeated across the lines of the same order may be intentional denormalization. The problem appears when the repeated attribute is interpreted as if it belongs to one grain, while the observed rows show that it varies at another.

This article assumes you already understand identifiers and selected keys. The focus here is narrower: use dependency violations as evidence that a descriptive attribute may be stored at the wrong grain, or that its determinant is missing part of the real business context.

sections.heading: A hypothetical order-line table
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail table named order_lines. Its declared analytical grain is one row per product sold on an order. In this fixture, order_id plus line_no identifies one row. The table repeats several descriptors so analysts can group sales without joining dimensions in every query.

Declaring the grain matters because every candidate fact or dimension attribute should be consistent with what one row represents. In this example, the row represents an order line, not a customer, not a product, and not an entire order header.
Here is the fixture, shown as rows rather than as a fully designed model:

1002, line 1, 2026-01-11, C002, Bo Chen, Bronze, P12, Water Bottle, Accessories, Nora, quantity 1
1003, line 1, 2026-02-05, C001, Ada Lim, Gold, P13, Floor Pump, Accessories, Nora, quantity 1
1004, line 1, 2026-02-08, C003, Cy Diaz, Silver, P11, Bike Light, Safety, Noor, quantity 1
1004, line 2, 2026-02-08, C003, Cy Diaz, Silver, P14, Gloves, Apparel, Mina, quantity 1

sections.heading: Expected dependencies to test
paragraphs: Before writing checks, state the dependencies you believe should hold. This step matters because not every violation is a modeling defect. Some proposed dependencies are simply false business rules.
For the hypothetical table, these are plausible expectations:
bullets: order_id determines order_date and customer_id. All lines on the same order should belong to the same order header.
customer_id determines customer_name, assuming this table stores a stable customer display name and not a historical name snapshot.
product_id determines product_name, assuming product names are stable for the reporting period or are represented by a current descriptor.
product_id determines product_category, assuming each product is assigned to one category in this simplified fixture.
customer_id determines customer_tier only if tier is treated as a stable customer attribute. If tier can change over time, this dependency should not be expected without a time qualifier.

category determines category_manager only if there is exactly one manager per category for the reporting period. If responsibility changes by date, region, or subcategory, category alone is not the correct determinant.

sections.heading: Illustrative SQL diagnostic
paragraphs: A dependency violation check groups by the determinant and counts the distinct dependent values. Any group with more than one dependent value is a counterexample to the proposed dependency.

The following is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL. It uses a VALUES fixture and common table expressions to keep the example self-contained. PostgreSQL documentation supports VALUES as a way to generate a constant table, common table expressions as temporary query-scoped result sets, and aggregate expressions such as COUNT(DISTINCT expression). No claim is made that this code was executed in a live database; the expected violating groups are worked through from the rows above.

codeExamples.code:
WITH order_lines (
    order_id,
    line_no,
    order_date,
    customer_id,
    customer_name,
    customer_tier,
    product_id,
    product_name,
    category,
    category_manager,
    quantity
) AS (
    VALUES
    (1001, 1, DATE '2026-01-10', 'C001', 'Ada Lim',  'Silver', 'P10', 'Trail Helmet', 'Safety',      'Lee',  1),
    (1001, 2, DATE '2026-01-10', 'C001', 'Ada Lim',  'Silver', 'P11', 'Bike Light',   'Safety',      'Lee',  2),
    (1002, 1, DATE '2026-01-11', 'C002', 'Bo Chen',  'Bronze', 'P12', 'Water Bottle', 'Accessories', 'Nora', 1),
    (1003, 1, DATE '2026-02-05', 'C001', 'Ada Lim',  'Gold',   'P13', 'Floor Pump',   'Accessories', 'Nora', 1),
    (1004, 1, DATE '2026-02-08', 'C003', 'Cy Diaz',  'Silver', 'P11', 'Bike Light',   'Safety',      'Noor', 1),
    (1004, 2, DATE '2026-02-08', 'C003', 'Cy Diaz',  'Silver', 'P14', 'Gloves',       'Apparel',     'Mina', 1),
    (1005, 1, DATE '2026-02-09', 'C002', 'Bo Chen',  'Bronze', 'P12', 'Water Bottle', 'Accessories', 'Nora', 2),
    (1006, 1, DATE '2026-02-12', 'C004', 'Dee Park', 'Bronze', 'P15', 'Energy Bar',   'Accessories', 'Mina', 5)
),
violations AS (
    SELECT
        'customer_id -> customer_tier' AS dependency,
        customer_id AS determinant,
        COUNT(DISTINCT customer_tier) AS distinct_dependent_values,
        STRING_AGG(DISTINCT customer_tier, ', ' ORDER BY customer_tier) AS observed_values
    FROM order_lines
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_tier) > 1

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        'category -> category_manager' AS dependency,
        category AS determinant,
        COUNT(DISTINCT category_manager) AS distinct_dependent_values,
        STRING_AGG(DISTINCT category_manager, ', ' ORDER BY category_manager) AS observed_values
    FROM order_lines
    GROUP BY category
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT category_manager) > 1

    UNION ALL

    SELECT
        'order_id -> product_id' AS dependency,
        CAST(order_id AS text) AS determinant,
        COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_dependent_values,
        STRING_AGG(DISTINCT product_id, ', ' ORDER BY product_id) AS observed_values
    FROM order_lines
    GROUP BY order_id
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) > 1
)
SELECT *
FROM violations
ORDER BY dependency, determinant;

sections.heading: Working through the results
paragraphs: The expected counterexamples are straightforward to verify from the fixture.

For customer_id -> customer_tier, customer C001 appears as Silver on order 1001 and Gold on order 1003. The dependency is violated because the same customer_id has two tier values. That does not automatically mean the data is wrong. It means customer_tier is not a stable customer-grain attribute in this dataset. It is likely a time-dependent customer attribute or an order-time snapshot.

The modeling response depends on the business meaning. If reports need the tier at the time of sale, then customer_tier belongs with an order-effective context, such as customer_id plus order_date or a customer-tier history table with effective periods. If reports need the current tier, then historical row-level copies in the order-line table can mislead analysts because old order lines will retain old values unless intentionally restated.

For category -> category_manager, the fixture has Safety managed by Lee and Noor, and Accessories managed by Nora and Mina. The same category has multiple managers. Again, the violation is a clue, not a verdict. Category_manager may depend on category plus date, category plus region, category plus subcategory, or an organizational assignment table. If the table presents category_manager as if category alone determines it, rollups by manager can shift responsibility in confusing ways.

The third proposed dependency, order_id -> product_id, also violates: order 1001 contains P10 and P11, and order 1004 contains P11 and P14. This is a useful counterexample because it is not a defect. It shows that order_id is a header-level determinant, while product_id lives at order-line grain. The violation tells you that order_id alone is not the grain of this table. If someone builds an order-level mart from this table and carries product_id along without aggregation rules, they are mixing grains.

Notice the difference between a helpful dependency and a bad one. customer_id -> customer_tier was plausible but failed, revealing a time-varying attribute. category -> category_manager was plausible but failed, revealing a missing assignment context. order_id -> product_id failed because the proposed dependency contradicted the stated order-line grain. All three results teach something, but only the first two are likely wrong-grain attribute candidates.

Expected violation: category -> category_manager, determinant Safety, values Lee and Noor.
Expected violation: customer_id -> customer_tier, determinant C001, values Gold and Silver.
Expected violation: order_id -> product_id, determinant 1001, values P10 and P11.
Expected violation: order_id -> product_id, determinant 1004, values P11 and P14.

sections.heading: Turn violations into modeling decisions
paragraphs: A dependency check should end in a modeling decision, not just a test failure. For each violation, ask three questions: what did we assume the determinant was, what determinant does the data suggest instead, and what should analysts be allowed to infer from this column?

For customer_tier, a better model might separate current customer attributes from historical order attributes. A customer dimension can hold the current tier if reports intentionally use current-state grouping. A customer-tier history table can hold effective dates if reports need point-in-time behavior. An order fact or order header can store tier_at_order if the business wants the exact value captured when the order was placed.

For category_manager, a better model might introduce a category_manager_assignment table with effective dates or other qualifying columns. The order-line table could keep category and join through order_date when manager-at-sale is needed. If manager responsibility is only a current organizational attribute and is not historically meaningful, the manager should usually be looked up from the current organizational structure rather than stored as a line-level fact attribute.

For order_id -> product_id, the fix is different. There may be nothing to fix in the source table. The issue appears when the table is consumed at order grain. If a downstream table has one row per order, it must aggregate line-level attributes or omit them. For example, total_quantity can be summed, but product_id cannot be selected as a single value unless the table is filtered to one-line orders or a rule such as primary_product_id is explicitly defined.

sections.heading: A practical checklist
paragraphs: Use dependency checks as lightweight model reviews during development, not only as production tests. They are especially useful when a wide analytical table has been assembled from facts, dimensions, and snapshots, because wide tables can hide grain mismatches behind convenient column names.

The workflow is simple. First, write down the declared grain in one sentence. Second, list attributes that look like they belong to a coarser or different grain. Third, propose dependencies in plain language. Fourth, run grouped distinct-count checks. Fifth, interpret each violation with the business meaning before changing the model.

Be careful with nulls. In PostgreSQL, COUNT(DISTINCT expression) counts distinct non-null values, and most built-in aggregate functions ignore null inputs unless otherwise specified. If null versus non-null is meaningful for the diagnostic, handle nulls explicitly rather than relying only on COUNT(DISTINCT column).

Also be careful with descriptive text fields such as names. A dependency violation on customer_name may be a spelling cleanup issue rather than a grain issue. The diagnostic finds counterexamples; the modeler still decides what those counterexamples mean.
bullets: If a dependent attribute changes for the same determinant, it probably has a finer grain, a time component, or a missing business qualifier.
If a proposed dependency fails because the determinant is too coarse, do not force the data to comply; restate the grain or choose the correct determinant.
If a downstream table changes grain, line-level descriptors need aggregation, exclusion, or an explicit selection rule.
If nulls are meaningful, include an explicit null-handling rule in the diagnostic.

takeaways: Functional dependency violations are practical counterexamples to grain assumptions in analytical tables.
A violation does not automatically prove bad data; it shows that the dependent attribute is not determined by the columns you thought determined it.
Wrong-grain fixes usually involve adding time context, moving the attribute to a dimension or assignment table, or removing the attribute from a coarser-grain output.

A deliberately false dependency, such as order_id -> product_id in an order-line table, can still be useful because it exposes where a downstream model is trying to carry line-level detail into an order-level table.

title: Composite keys in business event data
description: A practical guide to deciding when several columns together identify one business event, using a hypothetical retail event fixture with counterexamples and diagnostic SQL.
primaryKeyword: Composite keys in business event data
relatedKeywords: Composite keys in business event data
lead: A composite key is not just a group of columns that happens to be unique in one extract. In business event data, the useful question is narrower: which columns together identify one occurrence of the event at the grain the table claims to store? This guide works through that decision with a small hypothetical retail dataset and several counterexamples.

sections.heading: Start with the event grain
paragraphs: Before choosing a key, write the event grain in one sentence. For example: one row represents one item line recorded on a point-of-sale receipt. That sentence is doing more work than the column list. It says the row is not one customer visit, not one receipt, not one SKU per day, and not one final order total. It is one item line event.

A composite key is appropriate when no single available column identifies that event, but a minimal set of columns does. In relational modeling, candidate keys are attribute sets that could be chosen as the primary key, and a composite candidate key uses more than one attribute. Minimality matters: if removing a column still leaves the rows uniquely identified under the business rule, the larger set is not the key; it is a superkey.

For event data, this decision depends on the source system’s numbering rules and the event’s business scope. Receipt numbers may reset each day. Line numbers may only be meaningful within a receipt. Register identifiers may only be unique within a store. Customer identifiers usually identify people or accounts, not event occurrences. A column can be useful context without being part of the event identity.

This article is not a general argument for or against surrogate keys. A warehouse may add a generated event_id for storage, joins, or ingestion mechanics. That does not remove the modeling question. If the business event is naturally identified by store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no, then those columns still describe the event’s business key or alternate key even when a surrogate is present.
bullets: Declare the row grain before evaluating uniqueness.
Use business rules about numbering scope, not only distinct counts in one extract.
Require the key to be minimal: every column must be necessary.
Separate event identity from descriptive attributes such as customer_id, sku, or amount.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer that records item lines from store registers. The source system assigns receipt numbers per register per business day. Within each receipt, line_no identifies the item line printed on the receipt. The proposed event table is pos_item_event, and the intended grain is one item line on one receipt.

The following fixture is deliberately small. It includes rows that break tempting but wrong keys. Under the stated assumptions, the expected composite key is store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no.

Rows 1 and 2 show that receipt_no alone is too broad because a receipt has multiple item lines. Rows 1 and 3 show that receipt_no plus line_no is still too broad because another store can issue the same receipt and line number. Rows 1 and 4 show that business_date is needed when receipt numbers reset on later days. Rows 1 and 5 show that register_id is needed when registers in the same store can issue overlapping receipt numbers. Rows 6 and 7 show that sku is not a safe substitute for line_no because the same SKU can appear twice on the same receipt as separate item lines.

Under the stated assumptions, the five-column combination identifies each row in the fixture. More importantly, each column has a reason to be present. store_id scopes the register. register_id scopes the receipt sequence. business_date handles the daily reset. receipt_no identifies the receipt within that register and date. line_no identifies the item line within the receipt.

The fixture also shows why sample uniqueness is not enough. In a quiet store, receipt_no and line_no may appear unique for a day’s extract. That does not make them an event key if the source rules allow the same pair tomorrow, in another store, or at another register.

sections.heading: Test candidates against counterexamples, not just counts
paragraphs: A practical key review starts by proposing candidate sets and asking what real or plausible case would violate each one. The goal is not to make every possible combination unique. The goal is to find the minimal set that identifies the event under the declared grain and source rules.

For the hypothetical POS event, receipt_no is rejected because receipts have multiple lines and receipt numbers repeat. receipt_no plus line_no is rejected because that pair is only meaningful within a broader issuing context. store_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no is tempting, but it is rejected if registers issue receipt numbers independently inside the same store. store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and sku is rejected because the same SKU can be scanned twice on the same receipt. customer_id, business_date, and sku is rejected because a customer can buy the same SKU more than once in a day, and because customer_id does not identify the register transaction.

The diagnostic SQL below is illustrative PostgreSQL-style SQL, not execution evidence. It checks whether a proposed key has duplicate groups in a loaded table. A duplicate result means the proposed key cannot identify one row at the declared grain. A zero-row result is not a proof by itself; it only says the loaded data did not contradict the candidate. You still need the source rules and counterexamples.

After a candidate passes the duplicate check, test minimality by removing one column at a time. If removing register_id still produces no duplicates in a small sample, do not immediately drop it. Ask whether the source rules guarantee receipt numbers are unique across all registers in a store for a business day. If they do not, register_id remains part of the key even if this extract happens not to expose the collision.
bullets: A duplicate group disproves a candidate key for the loaded data.
No duplicates in one sample do not prove the business rule.
A key column is justified by the event’s numbering scope, not by habit.
Minimality is tested against rules and plausible counterexamples, not only against today’s file.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style diagnostic: find duplicate groups for the proposed key.
select
  store_id,
  register_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no,
  count(*) as row_count
from pos_item_event
group by
  store_id,
  register_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no
having count(*) > 1;

-- Counterexample check: show why receipt_no plus line_no is not enough.
select
  receipt_no,
  line_no,
  count(*) as row_count
from pos_item_event
group by receipt_no, line_no
having count(*) > 1;

-- Minimality probe: if this returns duplicates, register_id is necessary in the loaded data.
select
  store_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no,
  count(*) as row_count
from pos_item_event
group by
  store_id,
  business_date,
  receipt_no,
  line_no
having count(*) > 1;

sections.heading: When the composite key needs another column
paragraphs: Sometimes the five-column POS key above is still not enough because the event grain was misstated. Suppose the table stores every register action, including sale, void, return, and price override actions. Now one receipt line may have multiple events over time. If the row is one register action, line_no identifies the line affected, not the action itself. The key may need event_type plus action_sequence, source_event_no, or another source-provided event discriminator if the source guarantees uniqueness at the required scope.

This is a grain problem, not a performance problem. Adding more columns to force uniqueness can hide the fact that the table mixes different event types. If sale rows and void rows are both present, decide whether the table is a line-item state table or an event log. A line-item state table might have one row per current receipt line and include status. An event log might have one row per action and use a different key. Both designs can be valid, but they answer different questions.

Another common change occurs when events are consolidated from several source systems. If two POS platforms both use store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no, those values may collide after integration. In that case, source_system or source_instance can be part of the composite key, or the ingestion process can map each source event to a durable enterprise event identifier. The modeling rule is the same: the key must identify one event within the universe of rows stored in the table.

Do not add mutable descriptive attributes just to break ties. Amount, product name, cashier name, customer segment, and loyalty status are usually facts about the event or related entities, not identifiers of the event. If changing a value would create a new key for what the business still considers the same event, the column probably does not belong in the event key.
bullets: If one receipt line can have multiple actions, line_no may identify the line but not the event.
If multiple source systems are merged, include the source scope or map to a shared event identifier.
Avoid using mutable descriptions to make a weak key look unique.
A wider key is acceptable only when each added column narrows the event’s identity.

sections.heading: Enforce and document the decision
paragraphs: Once the key is chosen, write it down near the model definition: one row per item line recorded on a POS receipt; identified by store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, and line_no. Also document the assumptions that make it true: receipt numbers are assigned per register per business day, line numbers are unique within a receipt, and the table stores item line records rather than every register action.

Relational databases commonly support primary key and unique constraints over multiple columns. In PostgreSQL, a primary key can span more than one column and requires the key values to be both unique and not null. PostgreSQL also supports unique constraints over groups of columns, but ordinary unique constraints allow multiple rows when at least one constrained column is null. If a composite business key is implemented as a unique constraint rather than the table’s primary key, the key columns should also be constrained to not null when null is not a valid part of the event identity.

In an analytical warehouse, the same idea may appear as a model test rather than a physical constraint. The important part is that the rule is executable somewhere. If duplicates appear, the failure should tell the data team whether the grain is wrong, the source assumptions changed, or the ingestion process duplicated an event.

A generated event_id can still be useful. Kimball’s dimensional modeling guidance describes single-column surrogate fact keys as useful but not required, especially for identifying fact rows during ETL operations. That does not mean the generated value should be the only recorded answer to the identity question. Keeping the composite key as an enforced or tested alternate key preserves the business rule and makes duplicate diagnosis possible.

A good composite key decision leaves a clear audit trail: this is the event, this is its scope, these are the columns that identify it, these are the counterexamples that rejected smaller candidates, and these are the tests or constraints that guard the rule.
bullets: Document the grain and the key together.
Preserve the business key even if a surrogate event_id is added.
Turn the key rule into a constraint, model test, or duplicate diagnostic.
Revisit the key when the table’s event universe expands.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-style constraints for the hypothetical table.
-- This is a modeling example, not a recommendation about physical tuning.
alter table pos_item_event
  alter column store_id set not null,
  alter column register_id set not null,
  alter column business_date set not null,
  alter column receipt_no set not null,
  alter column line_no set not null;

alter table pos_item_event
add constraint pos_item_event_business_key
unique (store_id, register_id, business_date, receipt_no, line_no);

takeaways: A composite key is justified when multiple columns are jointly necessary to identify one event at the declared grain.
Counterexamples are the fastest way to reject attractive but wrong keys, such as receipt_no plus line_no when numbers repeat by store, register, or date.
Sample uniqueness is not enough. Use source numbering rules, plausible collisions, and minimality checks before accepting a composite key.
Generated surrogate identifiers can coexist with composite business keys, but they should not erase the documented event identity rule.

title: Set semantics versus bag semantics in SQL
description: A practical guide to showing why duplicate rows survive ordinary SQL queries, using a small hypothetical retail dataset and grain-based diagnostics.
primaryKeyword: Set semantics versus bag semantics in SQL
relatedKeywords: Set semantics versus bag semantics in SQL
lead: SQL looks relational, but ordinary SELECT queries do not behave like pure set operations. Unless a query asks for duplicate elimination, SQL can preserve duplicate rows. That matters when a join, projection, or report appears to be duplicating data. Often the query is doing exactly what bag semantics say it should do.

sections.heading: The reader problem: the same-looking row appears twice
paragraphs: A common debugging moment in analytics engineering is seeing the same customer, product, or date repeated in a result and asking whether SQL made a mistake. The short answer is no: ordinary SQL query results often use bag semantics, also called multiset semantics. A bag can contain two rows with the same values. A mathematical set cannot.

Relational theory is usually introduced with sets. In set semantics, a relation has no duplicate tuples. SQL tables and query results can contain duplicate rows unless constraints or query operators prevent them. PostgreSQL's SELECT documentation makes the default explicit: SELECT ALL is the default and returns all candidate rows, including duplicates, while SELECT DISTINCT eliminates duplicate rows from the result.

A primary key can prevent duplicate identifiers in a base table. A UNIQUE constraint can prevent duplicate values for selected columns. Neither kind of constraint says that every SELECT result must be duplicate-free. This article uses PostgreSQL documentation as a concrete reference for the SQL behavior discussed here; other database systems have dialect details, but the modeling lesson is not PostgreSQL-specific.

This distinction is not an engine tuning issue. It is a modeling and query semantics issue. The practical skill is to identify the grain of each intermediate result: what one row represents at that point in the query. If the grain is one order line, then seeing a customer repeated across multiple rows is expected. If the desired grain is one customer, the query must aggregate, filter, or deduplicate intentionally.

sections.heading: A small hypothetical retail fixture
paragraphs: Use this hypothetical retail dataset. It is deliberately small enough to reason about by inspection. The important assumption is that declared identifiers are unique at their natural grain: one row per customer, one row per order, and one row per order line within an order.
The fixture avoids null-specific behavior. Every foreign key value shown has a matching parent row. The goal is only to show why ordinary projection and joins preserve duplicate-looking rows.
bullets: customers has grain one row per customer.
orders has grain one row per order.
order_lines has grain one row per line item on an order.
A customer may place many orders, and an order may have many lines.

sections.heading: Projection in SQL is not set projection unless you ask
paragraphs: Start with the simplest counterexample: select only customer_id from orders. The orders table has three rows. Two of those rows belong to customer C1. In relational algebra under set semantics, projecting only customer_id would produce the set of customer identifiers: C1 and C2. Ordinary SQL projection does not do that unless duplicate elimination is requested. It returns one output row for each qualifying input row, with only the requested column retained.

The expected result has three rows: C1, C1, and C2. The two C1 rows are not contradictory. They represent two different input orders after the order_id column has been removed from the output. Once order_id is no longer visible, two rows can have the same displayed values while still being the result of two distinct input rows.

Adding DISTINCT changes the operator. It asks SQL to eliminate duplicate rows across the selected columns. The expected distinct result has two rows: C1 and C2. That is useful when the question is which customers have placed at least one order. It is wrong if the question is how many orders are represented, because it discards multiplicity.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative query. Expected rows are C1, C1, C2.
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id;

-- Illustrative query with explicit duplicate elimination.
-- Expected rows are C1, C2.
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id;

sections.heading: Joins preserve every matching combination
paragraphs: Joins are the second place where bag semantics surprise people. A join does not produce one row per customer just because customers is part of the query. It produces rows according to the matches between the joined inputs. PostgreSQL's table expression documentation describes an inner join as producing a row for each row in one input and each row in the other input that satisfies the join condition.

Join customers to orders. Customer C1 matches two orders, so C1 appears twice. Customer C2 matches one order, so C2 appears once. Nothing is duplicated accidentally; the result grain is one row per order with customer attributes attached.

Now join through order_lines. Order O10 has two lines, O11 has one line, and O12 has one line. The result grain becomes one row per order line with customer and order attributes attached. Ada appears three times because Ada has three order lines across two orders. Ben appears once because Ben has one order line. If the query selects only customer_name, the output may look like duplicate customer rows, but the hidden grain is still order line.
This is the main diagnostic move: do not ask first whether duplicates exist. Ask what the query's row grain is. A repeated value is only an error if it violates the intended grain.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative query. Expected result grain: one row per order.
-- Ada appears for O10 and O11; Ben appears for O12.
SELECT c.customer_name, o.order_id
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_name, o.order_id;

-- Illustrative query. Expected result grain: one row per order line.
-- Rows: Ada/O10/1, Ada/O10/2, Ada/O11/1, Ben/O12/1.
SELECT c.customer_name, l.order_id, l.line_no, l.sku, l.quantity
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_lines AS l
  ON l.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY c.customer_name, l.order_id, l.line_no;

sections.heading: Counterexample: DISTINCT can hide the wrong problem
paragraphs: Suppose a report wants one row per customer with two metrics: number of orders and number of order lines. A tempting but unsafe reaction to repeated customer rows is to add DISTINCT to the final SELECT. That may make the display shorter, but it does not answer the metric question. It can also hide a many-to-many join path that inflated counts before the final projection.

A better pattern is to aggregate at the intended grain before joining result sets. For this fixture, count orders per customer from orders, count lines per customer by joining orders to order_lines, then join the two customer-grain summaries. The Kimball Group's multipass SQL guidance addresses a related dimensional modeling concern: do not combine separate fact streams by directly joining fact tables across their foreign keys; instead, produce separately aggregated answer sets and align them at a common grain.

The arithmetic is checkable by inspection. C1 has orders O10 and O11, so order_count is 2. C1 has lines O10-1, O10-2, and O11-1, so line_count is 3. C2 has order O12 and line O12-1, so both counts are 1. The final customer-grain result should therefore be C1: 2 orders and 3 lines; C2: 1 order and 1 line.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative customer-grain metrics by aggregating before the final join.
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
),
line_counts AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS line_count
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_lines AS l
    ON l.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.customer_name,
       oc.order_count,
       lc.line_count
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN order_counts AS oc
  ON oc.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN line_counts AS lc
  ON lc.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- Expected rows from the hypothetical fixture:
-- C1, Ada, 2, 3
-- C2, Ben, 1, 1

sections.heading: A diagnostic for duplicate-looking rows
paragraphs: When a result has duplicate-looking rows, compare the displayed row count with the count at the intended key. This is a semantics diagnostic, not a performance prescription. It helps separate three cases: expected multiplicity, missing key columns in the SELECT list, and a genuinely unintended join path.

For the order-line join above, the physical result has four rows. If the intended grain is customer, the same result contains only two distinct customer_ids. That mismatch is not automatically a bug, but it proves that the current query is not customer-grain. If the intended grain is order line, then the key is order_id plus line_no, and the four rows are exactly right.

Constraints help make this reasoning reliable. A primary key on customers states that customer_id identifies one customer row. A primary key on order_lines states that order_id plus line_no identifies one line row. PostgreSQL's constraint documentation describes primary keys and unique constraints as mechanisms for enforcing uniqueness. The key point for modeling is that uniqueness belongs to declared or inferred grains; it does not magically propagate to every projection of a query.
bullets: Name the intended grain in one sentence: one row per customer, order, order line, day, or other entity.
List the columns that identify that grain.
Count result rows and count distinct grain keys.
If result rows exceed distinct grain keys, inspect joins and projections before adding DISTINCT.
Use DISTINCT only when duplicate elimination is part of the question, not as a reflexive cleanup step.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostic: compare result rows with customer-grain rows.
WITH result AS (
  SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, l.order_id, l.line_no
  FROM customers AS c
  JOIN orders AS o
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  JOIN order_lines AS l
    ON l.order_id = o.order_id
)
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS result_rows,
  COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS distinct_customers,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS rows_above_customer_grain
FROM result;

-- From the fixture, result_rows is 4, distinct_customers is 2,
-- and rows_above_customer_grain is 2.
-- That says the result is not one row per customer.

sections.heading: The practical rule
paragraphs: In SQL, duplicate rows survive ordinary relational queries because SQL generally operates on bags. SELECT ALL is the default behavior in PostgreSQL's SELECT syntax, and DISTINCT is the explicit request to remove duplicate rows. Projection can remove the columns that made rows distinguishable. Joins form rows for matching combinations. GROUP BY and properly chosen aggregation are explicit changes to that behavior because they state a grouping grain.

This is why the query duplicated my customers is often an imprecise diagnosis. More precise language is: the query is at order-line grain, but I selected customer columns; the join path creates multiple matches per intended key; or I need a customer-grain aggregate before the final join. That phrasing points to the fix without erasing meaningful multiplicity.

takeaways: Ordinary SQL uses bag semantics: duplicate-looking rows can survive projection and joins unless duplicate elimination is explicitly requested.
A repeated value is not necessarily a duplicate entity. Determine the row grain before deciding whether the result is wrong.
DISTINCT is correct when the question requires unique selected rows, but it can hide grain mistakes and inflated intermediate results.
Primary keys and unique constraints enforce uniqueness in base tables or declared column sets; they do not guarantee every query result is duplicate-free.
For mixed-grain metrics, aggregate each input to the intended common grain before joining the summaries.

title: First normal form and repeating groups
description: A practical guide to reshaping repeating attributes into child tables while preserving the parent key, using a small hypothetical retail-order example with counterexamples and diagnostics.
primaryKeyword: First normal form and repeating groups
relatedKeywords: First normal form and repeating groups
lead: Repeating attributes are easy to create and painful to query. A table with item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku looks convenient until a fourth item appears, an item needs its own status, or an analyst must count products across orders. First normal form is the point where you stop hiding a set of child facts inside one parent row. The practical move is not just to split columns out. It is to split them out while carrying the parent key and a clear child grain with them.

sections.heading: The modeling problem: repeated facts inside one row
paragraphs: First normal form is commonly described as requiring a single value at each row-and-column intersection and removing repeating groups from unnormalized data. For practitioners, the useful diagnostic is direct: if the same kind of fact appears multiple times in one row, and the column names differ mainly by a suffix or position, you probably have a repeating group.

Consider this hypothetical retail-order extract. It is not a benchmark, production example, or claim about a real implementation. It is a small fixture for reasoning about keys and relationships. The business event is an order. Each order can contain zero or more purchased products. A compact spreadsheet-style design might store the first three products directly on the order row.

This design appears to preserve the order because every product column sits beside order_id. But the relationship is only implicit. The parent order is mixed with several child item occurrences. The table’s candidate key may be order_id, but order_id does not identify a single product occurrence. It identifies a row that may contain several product facts.
bullets: Parent grain: one row per order.
Hidden child grain: one product occurrence within an order.
Symptom: item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku are the same attribute repeated by position.
Risk: the design has no stable place for the fourth item, item-level status, item-level discount, or item-level return reason.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL; not executed here.
-- Hypothetical denormalized order extract.
-- The numbered item columns are the repeating group.
CREATE TABLE order_extract_bad (
  order_id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date      DATE NOT NULL,
  customer_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  item_1_sku      TEXT,
  item_1_qty      INTEGER,
  item_1_price    NUMERIC(10,2),
  item_2_sku      TEXT,
  item_2_qty      INTEGER,
  item_2_price    NUMERIC(10,2),
  item_3_sku      TEXT,
  item_3_qty      INTEGER,
  item_3_price    NUMERIC(10,2)
);

INSERT INTO order_extract_bad VALUES
  (1001, DATE '2026-10-01', 501, 'MUG-BLUE', 2, 8.00, 'TEA-EARL', 1, 12.50, NULL, NULL, NULL),
  (1002, DATE '2026-10-01', 502, 'MUG-BLUE', 1, 8.00, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL),
  (1003, DATE '2026-10-02', 501, 'INFUSER', 1, 6.00, 'TEA-GRN', 2, 11.00, 'HONEY', 1, 5.50);

sections.heading: Counterexamples: two ways to split the columns incorrectly
paragraphs: The fix is not merely to make a taller table. The fix is to preserve the parent relationship and define the child key. Two common counterexamples show why.

The first counterexample is to create an item table without order_id. This produces a bag of item facts, but no fact states which order contained which item. The parent-child relationship has been discarded. You can count sku values, but you cannot reconstruct order 1001.

The second counterexample is to create a child table with order_id and sku only, treating those two columns as the key. That fails when the same product can appear twice on an order for different reasons. For example, a customer might buy one mug at full price and another through a promotion in the same order, or a source system might record separate item rows because they came from different fulfillment locations. Whether that can happen is a business rule. The data model should not accidentally prohibit it unless the rule is explicit.

A safer child grain is one row per order line. The line is identified by the parent order_id plus a line_number assigned by the source or by the ingestion process according to a deterministic rule. Now the row has an address: order 1003, line 2. The sku is an attribute of that line, not necessarily the identifier of the relationship itself.
bullets: Bad split 1: store sku, quantity, and price in a separate table but omit order_id. The parent relationship is lost.
Bad split 2: use order_id plus sku as the key when the same sku can occur more than once per order.
Better split: use order_id plus a child discriminator such as line_number, then store sku, quantity, and price as attributes of that child row.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL; not executed here.
-- Counterexample: this table has item facts but no parent order.
CREATE TABLE order_item_orphan_bad (
  sku        TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  unit_price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Counterexample: this key may be too narrow if a sku can appear twice on one order.
CREATE TABLE order_item_key_too_narrow_bad (
  order_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sku        TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  unit_price NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)
);

sections.heading: A 1NF reshape that keeps the parent-child relationship
paragraphs: A first-normal-form reshape separates the parent order facts from the repeating item facts. The order table keeps facts that occur once per order: order date and customer id. The order_line table keeps facts that occur once per product occurrence within an order: sku, quantity, and unit price. The foreign key from order_line.order_id to orders.order_id is the preserved parent relationship.

This is not just cleaner column naming. It changes what the keys can say. orders.order_id identifies one order. order_line.order_id plus order_line.line_number identifies one line on that order. The model can now represent one item, three items, or thirty items without altering the table definition. It can also attach future line-level facts, such as fulfillment_status or return_reason, without adding item_1_return_reason, item_2_return_reason, and so on.

Here is the same hypothetical data reshaped. The line counts follow from the fixture: order 1001 has two non-null item slots, order 1002 has one, and order 1003 has three, for six order_line rows total. The relationship is not lost because every child row carries order_id.
bullets: Parent table grain: one row per order.
Child table grain: one row per order line.
Parent key: order_id.
Child key: order_id plus line_number.
Relationship: order_line.order_id references orders.order_id.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL; not executed here.
-- Hypothetical 1NF reshape using PostgreSQL-compatible syntax.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date  DATE NOT NULL,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_line (
  order_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  line_number INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sku         TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price  NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_number)
);

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (1001, DATE '2026-10-01', 501),
  (1002, DATE '2026-10-01', 502),
  (1003, DATE '2026-10-02', 501);

INSERT INTO order_line VALUES
  (1001, 1, 'MUG-BLUE', 2, 8.00),
  (1001, 2, 'TEA-EARL', 1, 12.50),
  (1002, 1, 'MUG-BLUE', 1, 8.00),
  (1003, 1, 'INFUSER', 1, 6.00),
  (1003, 2, 'TEA-GRN', 2, 11.00),
  (1003, 3, 'HONEY', 1, 5.50);

sections.heading: How the reshaped model answers the original questions
paragraphs: After the reshape, ordinary joins recover the combined view when needed. The parent relationship is not encoded in column names. It is represented by a foreign key and used in a join predicate. PostgreSQL 18 documentation describes a joined table as a table derived from two input tables according to the join type, with the join condition determining which rows from the two source tables match. The same relational idea applies here: combine orders and order_line where their order_id values match.

The line-level table also makes aggregations less fragile. In the denormalized table, counting units of MUG-BLUE requires checking item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku separately, then remembering to update the query when item_4_sku appears. In the reshaped table, sku is one column and each line is one row.

Using the fixture above, the total units by sku are: MUG-BLUE equals 3 units, TEA-EARL equals 1, INFUSER equals 1, TEA-GRN equals 2, and HONEY equals 1. The order revenue arithmetic is also direct: order 1001 is 28.50, order 1002 is 8.00, and order 1003 is 33.50. These values come from quantity multiplied by unit_price on the six child rows, not from executing the illustrative SQL.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL; not executed here.
-- Reconstruct an order with its lines.
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.order_date,
  o.customer_id,
  l.line_number,
  l.sku,
  l.quantity,
  l.unit_price
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_line AS l
  ON l.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id, l.line_number;

-- Count units by product across all orders.
SELECT
  sku,
  SUM(quantity) AS units_sold
FROM order_line
GROUP BY sku
ORDER BY sku;

-- Expected arithmetic from the hypothetical fixture:
-- HONEY: 1
-- INFUSER: 1
-- MUG-BLUE: 3
-- TEA-EARL: 1
-- TEA-GRN: 2

-- Compute order revenue without scanning numbered item columns.
SELECT
  order_id,
  SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_revenue
FROM order_line
GROUP BY order_id
ORDER BY order_id;

-- Expected arithmetic from the hypothetical fixture:
-- 1001: 28.50
-- 1002: 8.00
-- 1003: 33.50

sections.heading: Diagnostic checklist for repeating groups
paragraphs: Use this diagnostic when reviewing extracts, staging tables, or early dimensional models. The goal is not to normalize everything for its own sake. The goal is to avoid hiding child relationships inside a parent row where keys and constraints cannot describe them.

First, inspect column names. Repeating groups often advertise themselves with numeric suffixes: phone_1, phone_2, item_1_sku, item_2_sku, contact_a, contact_b. A suffix is not automatically wrong. For example, billing_address and shipping_address may be two distinct roles rather than a repeating group. The question is whether the columns contain the same kind of fact repeated by position.

Second, ask what the smallest identifiable fact is. If the table is one row per order, but several columns describe individual products, the table is carrying two grains. Write both grains down before changing the schema. If you cannot name the child grain, the split will likely be unstable.

Third, preserve the parent key. A repeating group normally becomes a child table, not a standalone list. The child table needs the parent identifier plus a discriminator that identifies one child occurrence under that parent. That discriminator could be a source line id, an ordinal line number, an effective timestamp, or another business-approved component. The choice depends on the real entity being modeled.

Fourth, avoid using null columns to mean absent child rows. In the bad order extract, NULL in item_3_sku for order 1001 means there is no third item. That is different from an unknown sku for a real third item. Nulls can be appropriate for missing attributes, and dimensional presentation models may use their own conventions for unknown or not-applicable values. They are a poor substitute for representing variable numbers of children. If an order has two lines, store two child rows.

Finally, decide whether the child order matters. In the example, line_number is part of the key because source line position is useful for identifying a line. If order does not matter, you may still need a child identifier. Do not assume that sku or email address is sufficient unless the business rule says duplicates are impossible within the parent.
bullets: Look for positional suffixes in column names.
Write down the parent grain and the child grain separately.
Carry the parent key into the child table.
Choose a child discriminator that matches the business rule.
Represent absent children by absent child rows, not by a fixed set of null slots.
Treat distinct roles differently from repeated positions.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and boundaries
paragraphs: This article is deliberately narrow. It does not cover second normal form, third normal form, or whether SQL query results behave as sets or bags. It also does not claim that every downstream table must be fully normalized. Analytical marts sometimes denormalize for usability or performance after the base relationships are understood. That is a separate decision from whether the source concept has a repeating group.

The practical tradeoff is that normalized child tables require joins. That is not a defect; it is how the model expresses a relationship that was already present. The important question is where the relationship should be explicit. In a durable relational model, parent-child relationships belong in keys, foreign keys, and rows, not in repeated column names.

A useful stopping rule is this: if adding one more child of the same kind requires adding one more column, the design is probably not in first normal form for that concept. Reshape the repeated attributes into rows, keep the parent key, and define the child grain before building additional logic on top.

takeaways: Repeating attributes such as item_1_sku, item_2_sku, and item_3_sku hide child rows inside a parent row.
A correct 1NF reshape carries the parent key into a child table and defines a child key such as order_id plus line_number.
Do not split repeated values into an orphan table; without the parent key, the original relationship cannot be reconstructed.
Absent children should usually be absent child rows, not null-filled numbered slots.
The purpose of the reshape is semantic clarity: one table grain for the parent and one table grain for the repeated child facts.
