title: Entity identity versus record identity
description: A practical guide to separating a durable business entity from the many records that observe, describe, or reference it, using a small hypothetical retail dataset and counterexamples.
lead: A row is not always an entity. In operational and analytical systems, the same customer, product, merchant, or account may appear in many records: orders, emails, returns, support tickets, address snapshots, and source-system extracts. Treating every record identifier as the identifier of the business entity creates duplicated entities, unstable metrics, and hard-to-explain joins. The fix is to model entity identity separately from record identity.

sections.heading: The core distinction
paragraphs: Entity identity answers the question: which business thing are we talking about? Record identity answers the question: which stored observation, message, event, or row are we talking about?

Those questions often have different answers. A customer entity may have one durable customer_id in a modeled data layer, while the same customer appears in many order records, profile snapshots, email-change events, loyalty-program records, and source-system rows. Each of those records needs its own identity because each is a distinct observation. But none of those record identifiers should automatically become the identity of the customer.

This distinction matters most when a table mixes two grains. A customer profile extract, for example, may look like a customer table because it contains name, email, phone, and address. But if the extract is generated daily, the row represents a daily observation of a customer profile, not necessarily the customer itself. If the same customer appears on Monday and Tuesday, the two rows are two records about one entity.

A useful test is to ask what a key uniquely identifies. If a key identifies a specific load row, message, transaction, or snapshot, it is a record key. If it identifies the business thing across observations, it is an entity key. Candidate keys and alternate keys are still important, but the modeling decision starts by naming the thing being keyed.
bullets: Entity identity is durable across many observations when the business says the thing is the same thing.
Record identity is scoped to one stored row, event, snapshot, transaction, or source message.
A source primary key may be an entity key, a record key, or only unique within one source context. Its name alone does not prove the grain.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with two kinds of identity
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retailer that receives customer profile snapshots from an ecommerce platform and order events from a point-of-sale system. The example is intentionally small so the identity errors are visible.

The profile snapshot table has one row per source extraction of a customer profile. The order table has one row per order. Neither table, by itself, proves the final enterprise customer identity. Each table is an observation source.
Here is the hypothetical data in plain relational form:
bullets: customer_profile_snapshot.source_customer_id is stable inside the ecommerce platform, but the table has multiple snapshots per source customer.
pos_order.pos_buyer_token is a token captured at checkout. It can repeat across orders, but it is not guaranteed to be the enterprise customer identifier.
email is an observed attribute. It can help match records, but it can change, be shared, or be missing.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical example data. This is illustrative SQL, not evidence of execution.

customer_profile_snapshot
snapshot_id | source_system | source_customer_id | observed_at | email                | full_name
------------+---------------+--------------------+-------------+----------------------+----------
S1          | ecommerce     | C100               | 2026-01-01  | alex@example.com     | Alex Rao
S2          | ecommerce     | C100               | 2026-02-01  | alex@example.com     | Alex Rao
S3          | ecommerce     | C100               | 2026-03-01  | alex.new@example.com | Alex Rao
S4          | ecommerce     | C200               | 2026-01-15  | sam@example.com      | Sam Lee
S5          | ecommerce     | C300               | 2026-01-20  | family@example.com   | Jordan Kim
S6          | ecommerce     | C301               | 2026-01-20  | family@example.com   | Taylor Kim

pos_order
order_id | source_system | pos_buyer_token | ordered_at  | email_at_checkout    | amount
---------+---------------+-----------------+-------------+----------------------+-------
O10      | pos           | T9              | 2026-01-05  | alex@example.com     | 40.00
O11      | pos           | T9              | 2026-02-10  | alex@example.com     | 35.00
O12      | pos           | T8              | 2026-03-12  | alex.new@example.com | 25.00
O13      | pos           | T7              | 2026-01-25  | family@example.com   | 60.00

sections.heading: Counterexamples that break naive models
paragraphs: A naive design might declare snapshot_id as the customer identifier because it is unique in the profile table. That fails immediately: S1, S2, and S3 are three records about the same source customer C100. If snapshot_id becomes customer_id, Alex is counted as three customers before considering orders at all.

Another naive design might use email as the customer identifier. That also fails in both directions. Alex changes from alex@example.com to alex.new@example.com, so one person can have two emails over time. Meanwhile, Jordan and Taylor share family@example.com, so one email can refer to more than one person. Email can be a useful observed attribute or matching signal, but the fixture shows why it is unsafe as the sole entity key.

A third naive design might use the POS buyer token as the customer identifier. In the example, T9 links two orders, but T8 appears when Alex uses a different checkout context. If the model treats token as the durable entity key, order O12 is separated from the earlier Alex orders even though the profile evidence suggests a relationship through the changed email history of C100.

These are not exotic edge cases. They are ordinary consequences of confusing observations with entities. A record can be true and still not identify the entity. S3 truthfully records that source customer C100 had alex.new@example.com on 2026-03-01. O12 truthfully records that an order used alex.new@example.com at checkout. The modeling question is whether those observations point to an already-known business entity, create a new one, or remain unresolved.
A clean model does not pretend the answer is inside one column. It gives records their own keys, entities their own keys, and identity assertions a place to live.
bullets: Unique row does not mean unique entity.
Repeated attribute does not mean shared entity.
Changed attribute does not mean changed entity.
A source identifier may be durable only within the boundary of one system.

sections.heading: A practical relational pattern
paragraphs: A practical pattern is to separate three concerns: raw observations, durable entities, and the evidence that links observations to entities. This avoids forcing every incoming row to be the customer record.

In the modeled layer, customer_entity represents the business entity. It gets a surrogate or durable internal identifier whose job is to group observations that the business currently treats as the same customer. The profile snapshot and order records keep their own record identifiers. A bridge or assertion table records which observed identifiers have been associated with which entity, under what rule, and during what period if needed.
For the hypothetical fixture, one possible modeled result is below. This is not the only valid answer; it depends on business rules. The point is the separation of concerns.

In this modeled result, E1 is the customer entity for Alex. It is linked to ecommerce source customer C100 and to two POS buyer tokens, T9 and T8, because the hypothetical identity rule accepts the ecommerce email-change history as sufficient evidence to connect the checkout emails. E2 and E3 remain separate customer entities for Jordan and Taylor even though they share an email, because the business rule does not collapse shared household email addresses into one person. O13 can be unresolved, linked to a household entity in a different model, or assigned only after stronger evidence arrives. The example below leaves it unresolved at the person-customer level.

This pattern also preserves explainability. If someone asks why O12 is attributed to E1, the answer is not hidden in a destructive merge of rows. It is represented as an assertion that can include source, rule, confidence, and dates. If the rule changes, the model can revise the assertion without rewriting the meaning of the original order record.
bullets: Record tables preserve what was observed.
Entity tables represent the business thing being modeled.
Assertion or bridge tables document why a record or source identifier maps to an entity.
Unresolved records are allowed; they are better than fabricated certainty.

codeExamples.code:
-- Hypothetical modeled layer. Illustrative only.

customer_entity
customer_entity_id | entity_type
-------------------+----------------
E1                 | person_customer
E2                 | person_customer
E3                 | person_customer

customer_identity_assertion
assertion_id | customer_entity_id | id_domain                    | observed_id | rule_name                            | assertion_status
-------------+--------------------+------------------------------+-------------+--------------------------------------+-----------------
A1           | E1                 | ecommerce.source_customer_id | C100        | source_customer_id_is_stable         | active
A2           | E1                 | pos.pos_buyer_token          | T9          | checkout_email_matches_known_email   | active
A3           | E1                 | pos.pos_buyer_token          | T8          | checkout_email_matches_email_history | active
A4           | E2                 | ecommerce.source_customer_id | C300        | source_customer_id_is_stable         | active
A5           | E3                 | ecommerce.source_customer_id | C301        | source_customer_id_is_stable         | active

-- O13 is intentionally not mapped to E2 or E3 by email alone.

sections.heading: Diagnostic queries for grain confusion
paragraphs: Before designing the final identity model, run diagnostics that show whether a proposed key behaves like an entity key or a record key. These queries do not prove business identity, but they expose contradictions that should prevent premature key selection.

The first diagnostic checks whether a supposed entity identifier appears in multiple records. Multiple rows are not automatically wrong; they may be expected. The important point is to name the grain. If source_customer_id has multiple snapshots, then a table keyed by snapshot_id is not a customer entity table. It is a profile observation table.

The second diagnostic checks whether a proposed natural key, such as email, maps to multiple source customers. That result does not mean the data is bad. It means email alone is not a safe customer entity key under this fixture.

The third diagnostic checks whether an order attribution join would duplicate facts. Relational joins return rows for matching combinations, so if one order row matches multiple profile snapshot rows, the joined result has multiple rows for that order. The issue is logical grain confusion before it is a performance issue.

The expected results for the fixture are straightforward. source_customer_id C100 has three snapshots. family@example.com appears for two ecommerce source customers. Order O10 and O11 would each match both S1 and S2 if joined to snapshots by alex@example.com without a date rule, duplicating order amounts in an aggregate. O13 would match both S5 and S6 by family@example.com, creating ambiguous attribution.
bullets: Look for repeated records per proposed entity key.
Look for one observed attribute pointing to multiple proposed entities.
Look for joins that multiply facts because they join observations instead of resolved entities.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative diagnostics, not evidence of execution.

-- 1. Does a proposed source customer identifier have multiple observation records?
select source_customer_id, count(*) as snapshot_count
from customer_profile_snapshot
group by source_customer_id
having count(*) > 1;

-- Expected from the fixture:
-- C100 | 3

-- 2. Does email behave as a one-to-one customer key?
select email, count(distinct source_customer_id) as source_customer_count
from customer_profile_snapshot
where email is not null
group by email
having count(distinct source_customer_id) > 1;

-- Expected from the fixture:
-- family@example.com | 2

-- 3. Would a direct email join duplicate or ambiguously attribute orders?
select o.order_id, count(*) as matching_profile_rows
from pos_order o
join customer_profile_snapshot s
  on s.email = o.email_at_checkout
group by o.order_id
having count(*) > 1;

-- Expected from the fixture:
-- O10 | 2
-- O11 | 2
-- O13 | 2

sections.heading: Design rules and tradeoffs
paragraphs: The main design rule is simple: do not let the arrival format decide entity identity. Source records arrive at the grain that is convenient for the producing system. A data model should make its own grain explicit.

A second rule is to preserve the original record identity even after resolution. If a profile snapshot is merged into a customer entity, keep snapshot_id. If an order is attributed to a customer entity, keep order_id. Analysts and engineers still need to audit the observation, reverse an assertion, handle late-arriving data, and explain metric changes.

A third rule is to model uncertainty rather than hiding it. If the business rule says a shared email is not enough to merge two person customers, then the model should allow an unresolved order or a lower-confidence assertion. Forcing every record into exactly one customer entity may make dashboards look complete while making them less trustworthy.

There are tradeoffs. A separate identity assertion table adds joins and governance responsibilities. Someone must define rule precedence, survivorship, conflict handling, and whether deleted or superseded assertions remain queryable. The payoff is that entity identity becomes an explicit model concept instead of an accidental side effect of whichever source table was loaded first.

This article intentionally stays at the relational semantics level. Physical tuning, indexing, and execution plans are separate concerns. The logical requirement comes first: know whether each row represents an entity or an observation about an entity. Once that is clear, performance work has a stable target.
bullets: Choose the entity grain before choosing the entity key.
Keep record keys even when records are resolved to entities.
Represent identity assertions as data when the relationship is inferred rather than inherent.
Permit unresolved and ambiguous observations when the available evidence is insufficient.

sections.heading: A short decision checklist
paragraphs: When reviewing a table, ask four questions. First, what real-world thing or event does one row represent? Second, can the same business entity appear in more than one row? Third, can the proposed entity key change, repeat, or be absent? Fourth, what evidence justifies linking this record to that entity?

If the row is one extraction, event, message, or transaction, give it a record identity. If the business thing persists across those rows, give that thing a separate entity identity. If the connection between them is inferred, store the assertion separately enough that it can be explained and revised.
That separation is the difference between a model that merely stores records and a model that represents the business entities those records describe.

takeaways: Entity identity and record identity answer different questions: what business thing is this, versus which stored observation is this?
A unique row key, source primary key, or repeated attribute should not automatically become the enterprise entity key.
Use diagnostics to find grain confusion, especially joins that duplicate facts or attributes that map to multiple proposed entities.
A robust relational design keeps observation records, durable entities, and identity assertions separate enough to audit and revise.

title: Optional relationships in data models
description: A practical guide to representing absent relationships in relational models without inventing default customers, employees, stores, or other fake entities.
lead: Optional relationships are ordinary parts of real data models. An order might not have a sales representative. A support case might not be linked to a known customer. A shipment might not have a return authorization. The mistake is to hide that absence behind a fabricated default entity such as employee 0, customer -1, or store UNKNOWN. A better model lets the relationship be absent while preserving the integrity of real entities.

sections.heading: The problem with default entities
paragraphs: Practitioners sometimes create fabricated rows when a relationship is optional. The employee table gets an employee named Unassigned. The customer table gets a customer named Anonymous. The store table gets a store named Online Unknown. Those rows make foreign key columns non-null, but they also turn absence into a fake business object.

That tradeoff is usually not worth it. A fabricated entity can be counted, grouped, joined, assigned attributes, selected in a workflow, and accidentally treated as real. If employee_id 0 means no sales representative, every query that touches employees now needs special handling. If a future analyst forgets the exception, the model answers a different question from the one intended.

The issue is not whether nulls should appear everywhere. The issue is whether the model distinguishes two different facts: a real related entity exists, or no related entity is associated with this row. A foreign key value should identify a real row in the referenced table. If there is no related row because the relationship is absent, do not invent one just to satisfy a non-null shape preference.
bullets: Use a real foreign key value when a real related entity exists.
Use absence in the relationship when no related entity exists.
Do not add fake dimension or entity rows merely to avoid nullable foreign keys or missing association rows.
If unknown, not applicable, not yet collected, and intentionally absent are materially different states, model those states explicitly instead of overloading a fake entity.

sections.heading: Hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order model. An order is always placed through a sales channel. Some orders are helped by a sales associate, but many self-service web orders are not. The relationship between order and sales associate is optional. The sales associate itself is not optional when the relationship exists: any associate_id stored on an order should point to a real associate.

The following PostgreSQL 18-style SQL is illustrative. It has not been executed here. The purpose is to show the relational shape, not to make a performance recommendation. PostgreSQL documentation describes primary key, foreign key, check, and not-null constraints; this example uses those constraint concepts to express which values are required and which relationships may be absent.

PostgreSQL foreign key behavior is also important here: a referencing row normally does not have to satisfy the foreign key constraint when the referencing column is null. If the relationship must always exist, the referencing column should be declared NOT NULL. In this model, associate_id is deliberately nullable because the relationship from an order to an associate is optional.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative fixture data.
INSERT INTO sales_channel (channel_code, channel_name) VALUES
    ('WEB', 'Website'),
    ('STORE', 'Store'),
    ('PHONE', 'Phone');

INSERT INTO sales_associate (associate_id, associate_name) VALUES
    (101, 'Rina Shah'),
    (102, 'Marco Lee');

INSERT INTO retail_order (order_id, order_date, channel_code, associate_id, order_total) VALUES
    (1, DATE '2026-10-01', 'WEB',   NULL, 45.00),
    (2, DATE '2026-10-01', 'STORE', 101, 120.00),
    (3, DATE '2026-10-02', 'PHONE', 102, 80.00),
    (4, DATE '2026-10-02', 'WEB',   NULL, 35.00),
    (5, DATE '2026-10-03', 'STORE', NULL, 60.00);

sections.heading: Read the null as relationship absence
paragraphs: In this model, retail_order.associate_id is nullable because the relationship from an order to a sales associate is optional. The null does not describe a mysterious associate. It says the order row does not reference an associate row.

That distinction matters in queries. If the question is total order value by associate, self-service orders should not be grouped under a fake person. They should either be excluded from an associate-specific report or shown as a separate absence category created by the query result, not by the entity table.

The following illustrative query uses a left join so orders without an associate remain visible. PostgreSQL documents left outer join behavior as preserving rows from the left side and adding nulls for the right-side columns when no matching right-side row satisfies the join condition.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative query: keep all orders and show the associate when one exists.
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.channel_code,
    o.order_total,
    a.associate_name
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN sales_associate AS a
    ON a.associate_id = o.associate_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;

sections.heading: Worked results
paragraphs: From the hypothetical rows above, the left join returns five orders. Orders 1 and 4 are web orders with no associate. Order 5 is a store order where no associate was recorded. Those are all absent relationships, but they may not mean the same business state. The model preserves the absence; downstream rules can decide whether to label the rows self-service, missing attribution, not applicable, or something else.

The expected result of the illustrative query is: order 1 has channel WEB, total 45.00, and no associate_name; order 2 has channel STORE, total 120.00, and Rina Shah; order 3 has channel PHONE, total 80.00, and Marco Lee; order 4 has channel WEB, total 35.00, and no associate_name; order 5 has channel STORE, total 60.00, and no associate_name.

The arithmetic is straightforward. Overall order value is 45.00 + 120.00 + 80.00 + 35.00 + 60.00 = 340.00. Order value attached to a known associate is 120.00 + 80.00 = 200.00. Order value with no associate relationship is 45.00 + 35.00 + 60.00 = 140.00. Because absence is represented directly, these figures are not polluted by a fabricated employee row.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative aggregation over the hypothetical fixture.
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN o.associate_id IS NULL THEN 'no associate relationship'
        ELSE 'known associate relationship'
    END AS associate_relationship_state,
    COUNT(*) AS order_count,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS order_total
FROM retail_order AS o
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

sections.heading: Counterexample: the fabricated associate
paragraphs: Now compare the same fixture with a common anti-pattern: add associate_id 0 to sales_associate and use it whenever an order has no associate. This satisfies a non-null foreign key design, but it corrupts the meaning of the associate table. The table now contains both people and a control value.

The fabricated row causes practical failures. A headcount query can count one extra associate. An assignment workflow can display Unassigned as if it were selectable staff. A data quality rule that checks every order has a valid associate will pass, even though the business relationship is still absent. A territory assignment, payroll export, quota model, access-control rule, or employee-history table may later inherit the fake row and require defensive filters everywhere.

The deeper problem is dependency. Facts about an order depend on the order. Facts about an associate depend on a real associate. A fake associate row mixes a relationship state into the entity table. Normalization guidance commonly emphasizes organizing attributes around the keys they depend on; putting not applicable or no relationship inside a referenced entity table works against that principle.

This is not just a theoretical concern. Normalization material often discusses the problems that arise when designers make up fictitious key values to force unrelated facts into one relation. In this article's narrower case, the fictitious key is not being used to form a whole-table key, but the modeling smell is similar: a placeholder key creates rows that look valid while representing absence rather than a real entity.

codeExamples.code:
-- Counterexample only: do not use a fake associate to mean absence.
INSERT INTO sales_associate (associate_id, associate_name)
VALUES (0, 'Unassigned');

-- This hides absence behind a fake entity.
-- The order now appears to reference an associate, but it still has no real associate.
UPDATE retail_order
SET associate_id = 0
WHERE associate_id IS NULL;

sections.heading: When to use null versus an association table
paragraphs: A nullable foreign key is usually appropriate when one row may reference zero or one row of another table. In the example, each order can have at most one current sales associate attribution, so retail_order.associate_id works as a nullable foreign key.

When the relationship itself has attributes, history, multiple participants, or a separate lifecycle, use an association table instead. Absence is then represented by no association row. For example, suppose an order can be reviewed by zero, one, or many fraud reviewers, and each review has a decision timestamp. Do not add reviewer_id_1, reviewer_id_2, or fake reviewer rows to the order. Model the review relationship as its own table.

The following illustrative design represents optional review relationships without default reviewers. An order with no fraud review has no row in order_fraud_review. An order with two reviews has two rows. A reviewer_id, when present in order_fraud_review, must identify a real reviewer.

codeExamples.code:
-- Orders without reviews are found by the absence of association rows.
SELECT o.order_id
FROM retail_order AS o
LEFT JOIN order_fraud_review AS r
    ON r.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE r.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY o.order_id;

sections.heading: Diagnostic questions for optional relationships
paragraphs: When a model contains values like 0, -1, UNKNOWN, N/A, Not Provided, or Unassigned in a referenced entity table, pause before accepting them. Some special values are legitimate domain members, but many are relationship states disguised as entities.

A useful diagnostic is to ask what would be true if the row were real. Can this customer place a future order? Can this employee transfer departments? Can this store close, move, or have inventory? Can this reviewer sign in? If the answer is no, the row probably does not belong in the entity table.

Also ask whether absence and unknown should be separated. If the business needs to distinguish no associate needed from associate should have been captured but was missing, add an explicit status or reason near the relationship. Do not solve that with two fake associates named No Associate Needed and Missing Associate. Those labels are not people.

For the hypothetical retail order, one possible extension is a reason column constrained to a small set of relationship states. This is only appropriate if the states are part of the business process and can be maintained consistently. In PostgreSQL, a check constraint is satisfied when its expression evaluates to true or null, so the example below explicitly requires a non-null reason when associate_id is null.
bullets: If the related thing is real, store its key and enforce the foreign key.
If there is no related thing, allow the relationship to be absent.
If the reason for absence matters, model the reason as an attribute of the relationship or referencing row, not as a fake referenced entity.
If the relationship can repeat or has its own facts, move it to an association table.
If reports need a display label such as Unassigned, create that label in the reporting query or semantic layer rather than in the entity table.

codeExamples.code:
-- Optional illustrative extension for the hypothetical order table.
-- This version backfills the existing fixture rows before adding the constraint.
ALTER TABLE retail_order
ADD COLUMN associate_relationship_reason text NULL;

UPDATE retail_order
SET associate_relationship_reason = CASE
    WHEN channel_code = 'WEB' THEN 'self_service'
    ELSE 'not_captured'
END
WHERE associate_id IS NULL;

ALTER TABLE retail_order
ADD CONSTRAINT retail_order_associate_reason_check
CHECK (
    (associate_id IS NOT NULL AND associate_relationship_reason IS NULL)
    OR
    (
        associate_id IS NULL
        AND associate_relationship_reason IS NOT NULL
        AND associate_relationship_reason IN (
            'self_service',
            'not_captured',
            'not_applicable'
        )
    )
);

sections.heading: A practical modeling rule
paragraphs: Model optional relationships directly. For a zero-or-one relationship, use a nullable foreign key when the relationship is absent and a valid key when it exists. For a zero-or-many relationship, use an association table and let no row mean no relationship. In both cases, keep referenced entity tables reserved for real entities.

This rule keeps joins honest. Inner joins naturally return rows that have the relationship. Left joins let you keep base rows while showing the optional relationship when it exists. Anti-join patterns, such as a left join followed by a null filter on the association table, can find rows without a relationship. These query patterns are clearer when absence has not been hidden inside a fabricated default row.

There are tradeoffs. Nullable foreign keys require query authors to understand outer joins and null-aware filters. Association tables require another join. Explicit reason columns require governance so their values remain meaningful. Those costs are usually smaller than the long-term cost of mixing real entities with placeholders that every downstream system must remember to exclude.

takeaways: Do not fabricate default entities such as customer 0 or employee Unassigned just to avoid optional foreign keys.
Use a nullable foreign key for an optional zero-or-one relationship, and use an association table when the optional relationship can repeat or has its own attributes.
If the reason for absence matters, model that reason explicitly near the relationship instead of encoding it as a fake row in the referenced entity table.
Remember that PostgreSQL check constraints treat a null result as satisfying the check; write optional-relationship checks so null behavior is intentional.
Outer joins, grouped labels, and anti-join diagnostics are query-time tools for working with absent relationships; they should not be replaced by polluted entity tables.
